1) Gross monthly income = SSDI $22,646/12 ($1,887.17) + pension $3,108/12 ($259.00) = $2,146.17. There is no earned income.
2) Michigan broad-based categorical eligibility (BEM 213, effective 2026-02-01). A food assistance group with gross income at or below 200% of poverty is categorically eligible. Only groups with a senior, disabled or disabled-veteran member whose gross income is ABOVE 200% must pass the net income and asset tests. 200% of the 2025 HHS poverty guideline for one person ($15,650/yr) is about $2,608/month. $2,146 is below that, so the household is categorically eligible. This holds whether or not SSDI receipt makes the head 'disabled'.
3) Federal rule 7 CFR 273.9(a): categorically eligible households 'do not have to meet either the gross or net income eligibility standards.' The net income test (100% of poverty, about $1,305) that the consensus applied therefore does not bind. Assets ($3,600) are also irrelevant: there is no asset test for categorically eligible groups, and Michigan's limit for other disabled groups is higher anyway.
4) Benefit computation (7 CFR 273.10(e)(2)(ii)(A)): FY2026 maximum allotment for one person is $298; the standard deduction is $209. The medical deduction is medical costs over $35 a month, for an elderly or disabled member.
- Narrow medical reading (premiums $2,600 + OTC $100): deduction $190, net $1,747.17, 30% = $524.
- ESI premiums added ($8,489/yr): deduction $672.42, net $1,264.75, 30% = $379.
- Every premium field added ($11,089/yr): deduction $889.08, net $1,048.09, 30% = $314.
No shelter costs are listed (no rent and no mortgage payment), so there is no shelter deduction. In every case 30% of net income exceeds $298, so the computed allotment is $0.
5) Minimum benefit (7 U.S.C. 2017(a); 7 CFR 273.10(e)(2)(ii)(C)): every eligible one- or two-person household receives the minimum, which is 8% of the one-person thrifty food plan. For FY2026 in the 48 states and DC that is $24. The household is eligible through step 2, so it gets $24 a month.
6) Annual amount: $24 × 12 = $288.
The FY2026 figures ($298 maximum, $209 standard deduction, $24 minimum) were published by USDA FNS in its August 2025 cost-of-living memo, effective 2025-10-01, before the freeze. The FY2027 figures take effect 2026-10-01 and fall outside the FY2026 period used here. The work rules do not affect the result: the head is listed as working 40 hours a week and receives disability benefits.

Under every reading the net income is high enough that 30% of it exceeds the $298 maximum, so the computed benefit is $0 either way. The answer turns on whether categorical eligibility waives the net income test. Under Michigan BEM 213 and 7 CFR 273.9(a) it does, because gross income ($2,146) is below 200% of poverty (about $2,608), and the $24 minimum then applies: $288 a year. Only a reading that wrongly applies the 100%-of-poverty net income test to this categorically eligible household gives the consensus $0. That reading fails when the narrow medical deduction leaves net income at about $1,747, above the roughly $1,305 limit. Under broader medical readings the net income test is passed anyway, and the $24 minimum applies with or without categorical eligibility. So I do not treat $0 as a reasonable reading of the law.
